units.text: Fix gross margin and delivery economics, not headcount: seven firm levers lift operating margin from 1.0% to ~2.6% by FY2028, and a second wave prepared now closes the gap to the 3.0% target.
Revised answer: the diagnosis holds, but promotions and delivery alone are not enough — the plan adds shrink, targeted labour and store exits, and needs a prepared second wave to reach 3.0%.
Target the plan must satisfy: operating margin ≥ 3.0% by FY2028.
Capital constraint: ≤ $25M one-time cost or capital, FY2026–FY2028.
Lender covenant: operating income ≥ $20M in FY2026.
Stores: no closure of a store with a lease beyond 2027 without a board vote.
Delivery: keep the delivery service in some form (owners).
Reaching 3.0% by FY2028 means adding ~$35M of operating income (gap to close +35.6, from 7.7 if nothing changes to the 43.3 target) — more than double FY2025's $15.3M.
Do-nothing bridge, $M: FY2025 actual 15.3; 2027 minimum-wage step (+4%) −7.3; delivery rate rise (+3%) −0.3; FY2028 if nothing changes 7.7.
Operating margin: FY2025 1.02% · FY2028 with no action ~0.5% · target 3.0%.
Baseline (do-nothing case): FY2025 cost ratios and sales scale held constant — no further erosion and no growth assumed (optimistic).
2027 minimum-wage rise (+4%) applied to the whole $181.9M labour bill (conservative).
Baseline assumes the third-party delivery provider's proposed +3% is accepted.
If FY2024–25 erosion continued, FY2026 would already be below the covenant.

Target base: 3.0% of pro-forma sales of $1,444M after exiting 6 stores (3.0% target = $42–43M). Margins on pro-forma sales: $1,503M (FY2025), $1,444M (firm plan, 6 stores exited), $1,415M (full plan, 9 exited).

Starting hypothesis (margin loss is a gross-margin and delivery-economics problem, not a wage problem; resetting promotions and repricing delivery, rather than cutting labour, would restore 3.0%) tested against seven conditions: 1 decline driven by gross margin and e-commerce, not wages — Supported; 2 extra promotion is not buying profitable traffic — Supported; 3 e-commerce loses money once fully costed — Supported; 4 delivery can be repriced without losing the customer base — Partly; 5 store hours can be cut 8% without raising shrink or hurting service (management view) — Not supported; 6 weak stores can be exited within the board's commitments — Supported; 7 the hypothesis levers are enough for 3.0% within $25M — Not supported.
Promotions + delivery give ~$13M; even all seven firm levers give ~$30M → ~2.6%; ~$5M more must come from a second wave.
Gross margin (−1.02 pts: more promotion and shrink) and e-commerce fulfilment (−0.84 pts) explain 79% (~80%) of the 2.35-point margin decline; store labour (−0.30 pts) explains only 13%.

Margin bridge FY2023 → FY2025 (3.37% → 1.02%), pts of sales / $M / share: gross margin −1.02 / −15.3 / 43%; e-commerce fulfilment −0.84 / −12.6 / 36%; store labour −0.30 / −4.5 / 13%; occupancy & energy −0.20 / −3.0 / 8%; other SG&A 0.00 / 0.0 / 0%; total −2.35 / −35.4 / 100%.
$M impacts = change in ratio × FY2025 sales of $1,503M; figures may not sum due to rounding.
Why the dollar view misleads: labour had the largest dollar rise (+$14.3M), but sales grew 5.8%; at FY2023's 11.8% ratio, FY2025 labour would have cost $177.4M — so only $4.5M is excess.
E-commerce fulfilment more than tripled: $5.2M → $18.1M.

Income statement as % of sales, FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025: sales $1,420.0M / 1,468.0 / 1,503.0 (+5.8%); gross margin 26.04% / 25.61% / 25.02%; store labour 11.80% / 12.00% / 12.10%; occupancy and energy 5.80% / 5.90% / 6.00%; e-commerce fulfilment 0.37% / 0.74% / 1.20%; other SG&A 4.70% / 4.70% / 4.70%; operating margin 3.37% / 2.27% / 1.02%.

The 1.0-point gross-margin loss is fully explained by more promotion and more shrink; private label offset less than a fifth of it (total explained −1.02 pts / −$15.3M = actual change 26.04% → 25.02%; residual 0.00).
Promotion mix: promo share 24.0% → 29.0% (+5.0 pts) × −14 pts margin gap = −0.70 pts, −$10.5M a year.
Shrink: 2.1% → 2.6% of sales (+0.5 pts) = −0.50 pts, −$7.5M.
Private label: share 17.0% → 18.5% (+1.5 pts) × +12 pts margin gap = +0.18 pts, +$2.7M.
Harlow is also funding more of each promotion itself: vendor funding covered 55% of markdowns in FY2023 but only 46% in FY2025.
Shrink is now 2.6% of sales ($39.1M): produce waste 45%, theft 35%, admin and receiving errors 20%.
Mix effects use the stated margin gaps (promo −14 pts; private label +12 pts), unchanged over the period.
Deeper promotion has not paid for itself: 38% of FY2025 promotional events lost money even after counting the extra units they sold.
~$53M of new sales needed (at 20¢ contribution) to repay the $10.5M a year that +5 pts of promo share costs (0.70 pts × $1,503M ÷ 0.20).

Testing 'promotions work': deepest-promo stores grew comps +1.8% vs +0.2% for the rest. Benefit: +1.6 pts of sales × 20¢ = 0.32 pts of sales in contribution. Cost: every extra point of promo share costs 0.14 pts of sales in margin. Break-even: those stores can carry at most 0.32 ÷ 0.14 = 2.3 pts more promo share. The chain added 5 pts; at that depth the comp gain repays less than half its cost (0.32 vs 0.70 pts).
The category team's result is correlation: stores were not chosen at random (and it measures sales growth rather than profit) — a claim in the pack not relied on.
ValuMart has opened 11 stores in Harlow trade areas; nearby Harlow stores ran comps of −4.2% vs +1.1%.
Despite more promotion, 'more expensive' perception rose from 33% to 41%; customers choose Harlow for fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%), not price.
Broad promotional depth is an expensive and weak defence; private label (+12 pts margin) and fresh are better ones.

Promotions: cut the loss-making events chain-wide, require vendor funding as a condition of each event, keep targeted depth only in ValuMart-exposed stores while their traffic is measured, and move the value message to private label.
Open question: how much promotion is truly needed to hold traffic — so the reset is staged and tracked.
Contribution of 20¢ per new sales dollar is finance's estimate (§7) and flatters promotional sales.

Productivity absorbed two-thirds of the 9.4% wage rise: wage +9.4% ($16.80 → $18.38) alone would have added 1.11 pts; hours per $1,000 −6.0% (7.02 → 6.60) took back 0.77 pts; store labour 11.79% → 12.13% of sales.
Total hours fell slightly (9.97M → 9.92M) while sales rose 5.8%; labour at FY2023 productivity would have cost $193.9M.
Shrink by store labour intensity, FY2025: Q1 (fewest hours) 3.1%, Q2 2.7%, Q3 2.4%, Q4 (most hours) 2.3%; chain average 2.6%.
The hours already taken out are showing up as shrink: shrink rose 0.5 pts as hours per $1,000 of sales fell 6%.
Q1→Q2: 0.4 pts less shrink. Q3→Q4: only 0.1 pt. Extra hours matter most where hours are thinnest.

Rebalance hours instead of cutting them across the board: managers in the leanest stores say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days; waste and receiving errors are 65% of shrink, so these hours protect margin.
Fully costed, e-commerce loses ~$10M a year (−$10.4M in FY2025, −8.2% of e-commerce sales), not the +6.1% margin reported — almost all of it in home delivery.

Economics per order, FY2025, $ (click-and-collect / home delivery): incremental contribution +5.76 / +5.76; picking −7.40 / −7.40; third-party delivery — / −13.80; delivery fee collected — / +3.10; net per order −1.64 / −12.34 (a home-delivered order loses ~$12, a click-and-collect order ~$2).
Orders FY2025 (thousands): 559 click-and-collect, 772 home delivery; annual result −$0.9M and −$9.5M.

Reconciling the e-commerce team's +6.1% (% of e-commerce sales): add third-party delivery net of fees −6.5 pts; count only the 30% of sales new to Harlow −7.8 pts; fully costed (finance view) −8.2%. Step 2 switches to finance's incremental method; the two methods are not fully comparable.
Break-even: delivery needs 94% of its sales to be new to Harlow; click-and-collect needs 39% (survey: 30%).
Delivered share of orders rose 45% → 58%, while fees fell from 26% to 22% of delivery cost (26% / 24% / 22% for FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025).
The problem is subsidised home delivery, not e-commerce as such. Freezing the service locks in the loss; repricing delivery and steering customers to click-and-collect attack it directly.
Incremental contribution = $96 basket × 30% new to Harlow (survey; 70% cannibalisation) × 20¢ (finance). Costs reconcile to Table 1.

E-commerce cost reconstruction, $M, FY2023 / FY2024 / FY2025: orders 453 / 865 / 1,331 thousand; delivered orders 204 / 450 / 772 thousand; picking cost 3.3 / 6.3 / 9.8; third-party delivery cost 2.6 / 6.0 / 10.7; delivery fees collected −0.7 / −1.4 / −2.4; net fulfilment cost (= Table 1) 5.2 / 10.9 / 18.1; e-commerce sales 42.6 / 82.2 / 127.8; incremental contribution 2.6 / 4.9 / 7.7; fully costed result −2.6 / −6.0 / −10.4 (the loss has grown every year).
E-commerce team's 6.1% × $127.8M = $7.8M; deducting delivery net of fees ($10.7M − $2.4M = $8.3M) gives −$0.5M (−0.4%) even before cannibalisation.
E-commerce team's +6.1% margin was not relied on: it leaves out third-party delivery and treats every sale as new.

Management's draft plan (8% labour cut and e-commerce freeze) would leave FY2028 margin near 1.1%, far short of 3.0%: $M 15.3 FY2025 actual, −7.3 2027 wage step, −0.3 delivery rate +3%, +14.5 8% store-hours cut, −5.6 added shrink (midpoint) = 16.6 FY2028 draft plan, against a 3.0% target ≈ $45M.

The cut saves $14.5M on paper, but the leanest stores already run 3.1% shrink vs 2.3% (2.6% on average); an 8% cut moves every store toward them: +0.25–0.50 pts of shrink = $3.8–7.5M (we expect $4–8M back as shrink; midpoint 5.6 shown), moving the average store halfway to fully onto the leanest quartile's 3.1%, before any lost sales.

Fresh and service: 58% of customers shop Harlow for fresh produce, and managers already skip rotation on busy days; every 1% of sales lost costs ~$3.0M. FY2028 margin ~1.1% is before any sales lost to longer queues or empty shelves.
Freeze: stops the e-commerce loss growing but keeps the −$10.4M a year.
Blind spot: nothing in the plan addresses promotions — the largest single cause (−$10.5M).
units.correct_version: Blind spot: nothing in the draft plan addresses promotions — the largest gross-margin driver (−$10.5M) and the second-largest single cause; by the deck's own bridge, e-commerce fulfilment (−$12.6M) is the largest single driver.

units.text: Covenant: the cut helps FY2026 on paper, but shrink and service effects arrive with a lag.
Management's $14.5M labour saving was not relied on: it is gross of shrink and service effects.
Of three options, only the margin-first plan reaches 3.0% while keeping home delivery and the owners' commitments.

A. Management draft — cut store hours 8%; freeze e-commerce at current size. FY2028 operating margin ~1.1% ($16.6M); one-time cost small (not specified); FY2026 covenant met on paper if the cut lands early; commitments kept; main risks shrink, service, fresh reputation, promotions untouched. Verdict: Reject.

B. Margin-first plan (recommended) — promotion reset, vendor funding, private label, shrink; targeted labour; delivery repricing; exit 6 stores; second wave ready. FY2028 operating margin ~2.6% on firm levers ($37.8M); ~3.4% with the full second wave; one-time cost ~$17M; FY2026 ~$25M: ~$5M headroom; commitments kept, exiting the 3 other stores needs a board vote; main risks traffic response to fewer promotions (ValuMart), vendor push-back. Verdict: Recommend.

C. Margin-first, click-and-collect only — as B, but close home delivery and keep click-and-collect. FY2028 ~3.0% on firm levers ($42.9M); one-time cost ~$17M; FY2026 ~$25M; breaks the 'keep delivery' commitment (needs the owners' consent); main risks customer backlash, weaker convenience position (44% shop for it). Verdict: hold as fallback if second-wave delivery pricing fails / wave 2 falls short.
Also rejected: matching ValuMart with deeper promotions — every extra point of promo share costs ~$2.1M of margin and has not repaired price perception.
Option C assumes 40% of home-delivery customers switch to click-and-collect (team estimate).
Seven firm levers across four areas are worth ~$30M a year by FY2028 (base 30.1; range 16.8–38.0, i.e. $17–38M) and reach ~2.6%.
Lever split: gross margin $16.9M (promotions, vendor funding, private label, shrink) · targeted labour $5.5M · delivery repricing $3.3M · exit 6 lease-expiry stores $4.4M.

Lever 1. Promotion reset: drop loss-making events, promo share 29% → 25%. Sizing: 4 pts × 14 pts × $1,444M = $8.1M, less 25% for lost volume = 6.1 base; range 3.0–7.6 (low: promo share −2 pts; high: −5 pts, FY2023 level). Evidence: Strong (event review). Start: Now.

Lever 2. Vendor funding of markdowns 46% → 50%. Sizing: implied markdown 25.9 pts; gap 14.0 → 13.0 pts on $361M of promo sales = 3.7 base; range 1.9–3.7 (low: to 48%; high: 50%, 55% is wave 2). Evidence: Medium (FY2023 level). Start: Now.
Lever 3. Private label share 18.5% → 21%. Sizing: 2.5 pts × 12 pts × $1,444M = 4.3 base; range 2.6–6.1 (low: to 20.0%; high: to 22.0%). Evidence: Medium (+0.75 pts/yr trend). Start: FY2027.

Lever 4. Shrink 2.6% → 2.3%, hours reinvested in lean stores. Sizing: 0.3 pts × $1,444M = $4.3M, less $1.5M of added hours = 2.8 base; range 0.7–4.3 (low: −0.15 pts; high: −0.40 pts). Evidence: Medium (quartile pattern). Start: FY2027.

Lever 5. Targeted labour rebalancing: −3% hours in high-labour stores. Sizing: 3% × $174.8M × 1.04 (2027 wage) = 5.5 base; range 3.6–7.3 (low: −2% hours; high: −4% hours). Evidence: Medium (Q3≈Q4 shrink). Start: Now.

Lever 6. Roll out tested delivery pricing; renew contract at −5%. Sizing: fee test $3.0M saved − $0.5M lost sales; contract $0.8M = 3.3 base; range 2.0–4.0 (low: test result −20%, no contract gain; high: test +30%, contract −5%). Evidence: Strong (10-week test). Start: Now.

Lever 7. Exit 6 negative-EBITDA stores at lease expiry. Sizing: $2.1M losses removed + 25% of $78.7M sales × 12% = 4.4 base; range 3.0–5.0 (low: less loss in the 6; high: more loss in the 6). Evidence: Strong (past closures). Start: Now.
Not levers: other SG&A held flat at 4.7% of sales throughout (not a cause); occupancy and energy rose 0.2 pts and is partly addressed by the store exits.

Levers 1–2 interact: vendor funding is sized on the smaller, post-reset promotion base, so the two are not double-counted. Vendor-funding sizing assumes the 14-pt promo margin gap is net of vendor funding.
Lever values are at FY2028 run-rate on pro-forma sales of $1,444M; the labour bill includes the 2027 wage step.

Low / base / high cases: total firm levers 16.8 / 30.1 / 38.0; FY2028 operating income ($7.7M + levers) 24.5 / 37.8 / 45.7; FY2028 operating margin (on $1,444M) 1.7% / 2.6% / 3.2%. Even the low case adds ~$17M of operating income; the high case reaches ~3.2% on firm levers alone. Cases vary one driver per lever.

Rolling out the tested delivery pricing ($7.99 fee, $100 free threshold) adds ~$2.5M a year and keeps the service: net fulfilment cost 18.1 → 15.1 (−3.0), contribution lost on lost sales −0.5, net gain +2.5 $M a year.

Fee test applied to FY2025 (FY2025 → tested pricing): delivered orders 772 → 703 thousand (−9%); click-and-collect orders 559 → 637 thousand (+14%); e-commerce sales $127.8M → $125.2M (−2%); fee collected per delivered order $3.10 → $6.40 (+$3.30); picking cost 9.8 → 9.9 (+0.1); third-party delivery cost 10.7 → 9.7 (−1.0); delivery fees collected −2.4 → −4.5 (−2.1).
Contract renewal (2026): +$0.8M — refuse the proposed +3% (worth $0.3M); target a 5% reduction on the smaller volume ($0.5M).
Still loss-making after repricing: each delivered order still loses ~$9.04 ($5.76 − $7.40 − $13.80 + $6.40); that is ~$6.4M a year — repricing fixes only a quarter of the e-commerce loss.
Next test (wave 2): ~$3M — pilot cost-recovery pricing or a paid delivery membership; halving the remaining delivery loss is worth ~$3.2M; grow click-and-collect, not subsidised delivery.
Fee-test changes applied to the FY2025 base; lost e-commerce sales conservatively treated as lost to Harlow at 20¢ contribution.
Exiting the six loss-making stores whose leases end by 2027 adds ~$4.4M a year without a board vote (6 of the 9 negative-EBITDA stores); one-time cost ~3.0 (allowance, $0.5M/store); payback < 1 year.

Store table, $M (6 stores / 3 other / all 9): combined sales 78.7 / 39.3 / 118.0; four-wall EBITDA removed on exit −2.1 / −1.0 / −3.1; sales moving to a nearby Harlow store (25%) 19.7 / 9.8 / 29.5; contribution on moved sales (12%) +2.4 / +1.2 / +3.5; annual operating-income gain +4.4 / +2.2 / +6.6; one-time cost ~3.0 / 7.5 (lease exit) / ~10.5; payback < 1 year / ~3.4 years / ~1.6 years.
The other three stores repay their exit cost in ~3.4 years (+$2.2M a year vs $7.5M lease exit) and require a board vote.

Stores sequence: Now — confirm store-level P&Ls, then give notice on the 6 lease-expiry stores. Next 6 months — test a fix (range, fresh, labour) in the other 3. Mid-FY2027 — bring the 3 to a board vote if the fix fails; this is part of wave 2 (+$2.2M).
Why not exit all nine now: the 3 need a board vote and $7.5M, 44% of the plan's one-time budget; a 3.4-year payback is slower than every other lever; a fix test is cheap.
Gain is likely understated: four-wall EBITDA excludes store depreciation, which also goes on exit. Allocated overheads stay, but four-wall EBITDA already excludes them, so the gain is not overstated.

The nine stores' sales and EBITDA are split pro rata (6/9, 3/9) because the pack gives only totals; the closure allowance is a team assumption. Pro-rata split is the main uncertainty: if the 6 carry less of the loss, the gain could be ~$3M.

Plan bridge, operating income $M FY2025 → FY2028: 15.3 FY2025 actual; −7.6 wage step & delivery rate; 7.7 if nothing changes; +16.9 gross-margin levers (1–4); +5.5 targeted labour (5); +3.3 delivery repricing (6); +4.4 exit 6 stores (7); 37.8 firm plan; +9.9 second wave; 47.7 full plan. Operating margin 1.0% / 0.5% / 2.6% / 3.4%.

Second wave (~$10M; total 9.9): exit the 3 other loss-making stores (board vote; $7.5M) 2.2; cost-recovery delivery pricing or membership (pilot first) 3.0; vendor funding from 50% back to FY2023's 55% 4.7.
The gap left by the firm plan is $5–6M (37.8 vs 3.0% target ≈ $42–43M), so about half the second wave must deliver (~$5M needed).
Prepare all three second-wave options now so the choice can be made at the mid-FY2027 checkpoint.
Four no-regret moves in the next 90 days lift FY2026 operating income to ~$25M, about $5M above the $20M covenant.

FY2026 operating income bridge, $M: FY2025 run-rate 15.3; promo reset +3.2; vendor funding +1.0; delivery pricing +1.7; labour +2.7; private-label trend +1.0; FY2026 24.9. FY2026 in-year values by lever 1–7: 3.2 / 1.0 / 1.0 / 0.0 / 2.7 / 1.7 / 0.0, total 9.6.
First move 1. Promotion reset: drop the loss-making events from the next calendar, worst first; minimum vendor funding per event.
First move 2. Delivery: roll out $7.99 fee / $100 threshold; renew the contract at no increase.
First move 3. Labour: replace the 8% cut with targeted rebalancing (−3% hours in high-labour stores; protect receiving and produce rotation).
First move 4. Stores: give notice on the 6 lease-expiry stores.

Roadmap FY2027: private-label push toward 21%; shrink programme to 2.3%, pilot in 10 stores first; fix test, then board vote, on the 3 other stores; pilot cost-recovery delivery pricing; press vendor funding toward 55%. FY2028: full run-rate.
Mid-FY2027 checkpoint: if run-rate margin is below ~2.4%, trigger the second wave in full and put the fallback (C) to the owners.
Why these four first: they pay back within the year, rest on the strongest evidence, need no capital or board vote, and can be reversed if traffic suffers.
units.correct_version: Why these four first: they need no board vote, most pay back within the year and they can be reversed if traffic suffers — but they are not capital-free: the firm wave carries ~$9.5M of one-time cost (e.g. $3.0M closure costs for the 6 lease-expiry stores, scheduling tools and training, promotion analytics). Evidence is Strong for promotions, delivery pricing and store exits but only Medium for targeted labour, and the store exits contribute $0 in FY2026.

units.text: Risk: if about a third of FY2025's $18M erosion recurs, the covenant headroom is gone, so track monthly and brief the lender early.

FY2026 in-year phasing (team assumption): promotions 50%, vendor funding 25%, delivery 75%, labour 50%, private label ~25% of run-rate; FY2025 scale. Delivery shown net of the half-year contract rise (−$0.2M).
The plan needs ~$17M of one-time cost — inside the $25M cap (FY2026–FY2028) with ~$8M of contingency.

One-time cost items, $M (basis; wave): lease exit, 3 other weak stores 7.5 (briefing pack Table 6; wave 2); closure costs, 6 lease-expiry stores 3.0 (allowance $0.5M per store; wave 1); labour scheduling and shrink tools, training 3.0 (allowance; 1–2); private-label range development 2.0 (allowance; 2); promotion analytics and vendor negotiation 1.0 (allowance; 1); delivery pricing changes and pilot 0.5 (allowance; 1–2); total plan 17.0; cap 25.0; contingency 8.0.
Firm wave alone needs ~$9.5M; the cap holds unless the allowances prove ~80% too low ((25 − 7.5) ÷ 9.5 = 1.84×).
Reinvested shrink hours (~$1.5M a year; ~78,000 hours, ~1 FTE per lean store) are an operating cost and are already netted in lever 4.
Only the $7.5M lease-exit cost comes from the pack; other one-time items are team planning allowances for the CFO to validate.
The answer is most sensitive to traffic response and vendor funding (key risks: ValuMart traffic and vendor push-back); each risk has a trigger, and the core diagnosis survives every test.

Traffic response to fewer promotions (ValuMart): base case 25% of gross gain lost; if wrong 50% lost; FY2028 impact −$2.0M; trigger: comps in ValuMart trade areas below −4.2%; response: keep depth in exposed stores, lead with private label.
Vendor funding recovery: base 46% → 50%; if wrong stays at 46%; FY2028 impact −$3.7M; trigger: funding share in next two promo cycles; response: drop events vendors will not fund.

Share of e-commerce sales new to Harlow (survey): base 30%; if 50%, loss shrinks to −$5.3M; trigger: customer-panel and loyalty data; response: none needed — delivery still loses $8.50 per order. Survey incrementality (30%) is stated intent; delivery is loss-making even at 50%.
Shrink responds to reinvested hours: base 2.6% → 2.3%; if wrong only 2.45%; FY2028 impact −$2.1M; trigger: 10-store pilot shrink vs control. Shrink-by-quartile is a correlation, hence the pilot.
Shrink programme: scale only if the pilot gains ≥ 0.2 pts.
2027 wage step: base +4% on full bill; if +6%, FY2028 impact −$3.6M; trigger: legislation, local market rates; response: scheduling productivity, second wave.
Loss split across the 9 weak stores: base pro rata; if the 6 carry less loss, FY2028 impact −$1.4M; trigger: store-level P&Ls; response: re-rank stores before giving notice.

FY2026 trading (no FY2026 data in pack): base holds at FY2025 run-rate; if erosion continues, ~$5M slippage uses up covenant headroom; trigger: monthly operating income vs $20M path; response: brief lender, speed up promotion cuts.

Robustness: under every row, gross margin and delivery remain the main causes and the 8% cut remains inferior; what changes is how much of the second wave is needed. Impacts are changes to FY2028 operating income versus the base plan ($37.8M firm).
Decision 1: endorse the margin-first plan in place of the 8% across-the-board labour cut — targets 2.6% on firm levers and 3.0% with the second wave; one-time cost ~$17M within the $25M cap.
Decision 2: approve the delivery repricing roll-out and an e-commerce guardrail — $7.99 fee / $100 threshold chain-wide; grow click-and-collect, not subsidised delivery; delivery itself is kept.
Decision 3: authorise preparation of the second wave — fix test and a board vote on the 3 other stores by mid-FY2027 ($7.5M); cost-recovery delivery pilot; vendor terms.
FY2026 covenant forecast; lender briefing — CFO — Week 2.
Next promotion calendar without loss-making events; vendor terms — Category / merchandising — Week 4.
Delivery pricing live chain-wide; contract renewed — E-commerce — Week 6.
Store-by-store labour rebalancing plan (replaces 8% cut) — COO — Week 6.
Store P&L review; notices on 6 lease-expiry stores — Property / CFO — Week 8.
Shrink pilot launched in 10 lean stores — COO — Week 12.

Quarterly scorecard of six measures, FY2025 → FY2028 target: promo share of sales 29% → 25%; vendor funding of markdowns 46% → 50%+; private-label share 18.5% → 21%; shrink, % of sales 2.6% → 2.3%; loss per delivered order $12.34 → < $5; operating income ≥ $20M FY2026, 3.0% FY2028.

Fiscal timing: the pack's latest actuals are FY2025 and its constraints (covenant, capital window, labour plan) start in FY2026, so FY2026 is treated as the first plan year. If FY2026 has closed by the board date, its covenant result is a fact to report and the in-year estimates apply to FY2027.

Team estimates not in the pack: one-time cost allowances (except the $7.5M lease exit); 25% lost-volume allowance on the promotion reset; $1.5M a year of reinvested hours; FY2026 phasing of each lever; 40% of delivery customers switching to click-and-collect under option C.
Analysis is based only on the board briefing pack (synthetic benchmark data); all figures $ millions unless stated; fiscal years end in January.
